full_judgment:
Mr. A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 15.04.2014 passed by the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 2013 arising out of Artha Execution Case No.156 of 2010 in disallowing the Miscellaneous Case filed under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Section 32 and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

2. The short facts for disposal of the instant appeal is that the appellant Bank Asia as plaintiff instituted Artha Rin Suit No.75 of 2005 before the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka against the Respondent Nos.2-6 for recovery of Tk.4,87,53,I99.5 I as on 31.03.2005 by selling the mortgage property.

3. The plaint case of Artha Rin Suit No.75 of 2005 in brief that the defendants were enjoying credit facility from the plaintiff Bank since 2001 by opening letter of credit and availing Term Loan, LTR, Over Draft, Term Loan Construction facilities that as security of the said Credit facilities defendant No.1 mortgaged 16.50 decimals of land by executing registered mortgage deed being No.8036 dated 19.06.2003 and registered Power of Attorney deed being No.8037 dated 19.06.2003, the defendants also executed Hypothecation of Fixed Assets and Letter of Hypothecation and other charge documents. In spite of repeated reminders and requests and legal notice the defendants did not come forward to adjust their liabilities, hence the suit.

4. The said suit was decreed in favour of the appellant bank by Judgment and decree dated 31.05.2009 (decree signed on 03.06.2009).

5. The appellant Bank thereafter filed Artha Execution Case No.239 of 2009 before the Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka to execute the decree passed in the said Artha Rin Suit.

6. The respondent No.1 IPDC on the other hand also instituted Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 before the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka against the Respondent Nos.2-6 for recovery of Tk.3,87,66,662/- only as on 31.01.2004. The present appellant Bank Asia i.e. Bank Asia Ltd. was also impleaded in the said suit as defendant No.5 and they filed written statement.

7. The plaint case of Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 in short was that the plaintiff financial institution sanctioned credit facility to the defendants in 1997, in the year 1999 the plaintiff and defendant No.1 executed a loan agreement containing several terms and conditions, defendant Nos.2-4 also guaranteed the repayment of loan, the defendant No.1 also executed a letter of undertaking, subsequently as per defendant Nos.1-5 requests the plaintiffs disbursed the loan to the defendant No. 1.

8. The defendant No.2 on 19 November, 2001 forwarded to the plaintiff 5000 shares of Mirpur Ceramic Works Ltd. as temporary security, in spite of repeated requests, reminders and legal notice the defendants did not adjust their liabilities, thereafter by legal notice dated 10 February, 2002 the plaintiff terminated the Loan Agreement with immediate effect.

9. The plaintiff on 4 April, 2002 invited defendant No.1 to come to a meeting to discuss matters relating to legal documentation. The defendant No.5 in the meantime communicated with the plaintiff and informed that defendant No.1 has approached them for grant of a loan while the plaintiff was considering pari passu security sharing with the defendant No. 5.

10. The defendant No.1 on 18 June, 2003 informed the plaintiff of its right to deal with its project land it deemed fit on the ground of the plaintiff's failure to release the interim security. The plaintiff on 26 June, 2003 notified the defendant No.5 of its prior claim on the schedule assets and personal undertaking of the defendant Nos.2-4.

11. The defendant No.5 in response to the plaintiffs letter dated 26 June, 2003 informed that it had allowed defendant No.1 to create registered mortgage over the defendant No.1 's assets in breach of the Loan Agreement and the undertaking defendant No.1 failed to execute and produce the documents, hence the suit.

12. The present appellant that is defendant No.5 filed written statements in the said suit contending that the suit is bad for misjoinder of parties, the defendant No.5 is neither a borrower nor a guarantor nor a mortgagor against the loan availed by the plaintiff and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. The Bank Asia Ltd. in its written statement further contended that on 27.05.2003 they requested the plaintiff to inform whether security interest over the defendant nots assets can be shared on pad passu basis, but the plaintiff never disclosed the security taken or to be taken against the credit facilities, the defendant No.5 as a result conducted due diligence on the records of the plaintiff maintained with RJSC, the plaintiff furnished Bank Asia Ltd. wrong information vide their letter dated r 06.11.2003 about the security taken against the facility extended by the plaintiff which was found false the plaintiff never disclosed to the defendant No.5, Bank Asia Ltd. the security obtained/to be obtained against the term loan limit.

13. The IPDC subsequently filed Artha Rin Suit and the said suit was transferred to the Court of learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka and renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010.

14. The said suit was decreed in favour of the respondent No.1 IPDC and against the defendant Nos.1-2 of the said suit and was dismissed against Bank Asia Ltd. i.e. respondent No.5 and 2 others by Judgment and decree dated 15.07.2010 (decree signed on 18.07.2010).

15. The learned Court while dismissing the suit against Bank Asia Ltd. observed that Bank E Asia Ltd. is a separate banking institution and not the principal borrower.

16. The respondent No.1 IPDC thereafter filed Artha Execution Case No.156 of 2010 before the Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka to execute the decree passed in the Artha Rin Suit.

17. The respondent No.1 IPDC thereafter filed a Transfer Miscellaneous Case No.162 of 2012 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka for analogous hearing and execution of both the execution case to a court having jurisdiction.

18. The learned District Judge ultimately allowed the transfer miscellaneous case by Iorder dated 02.07.2012 and withdrawn Artha Execution Case No.239 of 2009 from the Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka and transferred the same to Artha Rin Adalat No.3; Dhaka.

19. The Artha Execution Case No.239 of 2009 after transfer has been renumbered as Artha Execution Case No.104 of 2012.

20. The respondent no.1 IPDC in the meantime filed an application on 30.05.2012 for stay before the Artha Rin Adalat No.2 and Artha Rin Adalat No.2 on 31.05.2012 stayed the Execution Case No.239 of 2009.

21. The proceeding of Execution Case No.239 of 2009 was stayed in view of filing Transfer Miscellaneous Case at the instance of respondent No.1 IPDC on 31.05.2012.

22. The respondent No.1 IPDC in the meantime obtained an order of attachment on 28.05.2012 in Artha Execution Case No.156 of 2010 attaching 24 decimals of land which includes 16.50 decimals of land which is under registered mortgage with the appellant Bank Asia Ltd.

23. The appellant Bank Asia subsequently filed an application on 22.07.2012 under Section 57 of the Artha Rin Ain for recalling the entire order of Execution Case No.156 of 2010 which were passed during pendency of Transfer Miscellaneous Case No.162 of 2012.

24. The learned Judge of the executing court after hearing rejected the said application by its order dated 04.02.2013.

25. The appellant as applicant thereafter filed the instant Miscellaneous Case on 11.04.2013 under order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Section 32 and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 for releasing the mortgaged land from attachment.

26. The respondent No.1 IPDC contested the said Miscellaneous Case by filing written objection.

27. The learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka after hearing disallowed the Miscellaneous Case by its judgment and order dated 15.04.2014 which is impugned herein.

28. The IPDC in their written objection in paragraph no.30 admitted that "in breach of the loan agreement and the undertaking the opposite party No.2 failed to execute/or produce the following security documents (a) a joint and several equitable mortgage in favour of the opposite party No.1 (IPDC) ranking pari passu over the opposite party No.2's immovable property by the deposit of the title deeds, the relative memorandum of deposit, a right to call for a legal mortgage" and after such admission the instant miscellaneous case No.20 of 2013 ought to have been allowed straight way but the learned court below without taking such admission into consideration rejected the miscellaneous case most illegally and arbitrarily.

29. It is stated that 16.50 decimals of land out of 24 decimals of attached land was under registered mortgage in favour of the appellant Bank by dint of Mortgage deed No.8036 dated 19.06.2003, that a registered power of attorney deed No.8037 dated 19.06.2003 was also executed in favour of the appellant bank and all the documents of title was also deposited and is still under the custody of the instant appellant and there is no security sharing or pari passu agreement between Bank Asia Ltd. and IPDC and the respondent No.2 did not execute any registered or equitable mortgage in favour of IPDC and therefore for all practical purposes the appellant has paramount right over their mortgaged property which cannot be circumvent in any manner.

30. It is stated that the reference of the title deed being No.22297 dated 15 February, 1968 which respondent No.1 IPDC has given in their plaint is not the title deed of respondent No.2 rather the vendor of the said deed is Bilkis Begum.

31. The case of the IPDC is that the IPDC sanctioned credit facility to Bangladesh German Food Limited (BGFL) in 1997. In the year 1999, IPDC and BGFL executed a loan agreement containing several terms and conditions and BGFL also executed a Letter of Undertaking on 21.06.1999 stating that it would submit all the security documents. As per request of BGFL, IPDC disbursed the loan amount. Mr. Yusuf Ali Tabani, Managing Director ("MD") of BGFL forwarded 5000 shares of Mirpur Ceramic Works Ltd. as temporary security. In spite of repeated requests, reminders and legal notice, BGFL did not adjust their liabilities. On 10.02.2002 IPDC terminated the Loan Agreement with immediate effect. On 04.04.2002, IPDC invited BGFL to come to a meeting to discuss matters relating to legal documents and time frame for payment of dues. In the meantime on 27.05.2003 Bank Asia communicated IPDC and informed BGFL approaches them to grant a loan and asked IPDC whether Pari Passu Security sharing over the BGFL's assets could be allowed to them. While IPDC was considering pari passu security sharing with Bank Asia, on 18.06.2003 BGFL, informed IPDC of its right to deal with its project land it deemed fit on the ground of the IPDC's failure to release the interim security. On 26.06.2003 IPDC informed Bank Asia of its prior claim on the schedule assets. In response to letter dated 26.06.2003, Bank Asia informed that it had allowed BGFL to create registered mortgage over BGFL's assets on 19.06.2003. In breach of the Loan Agreement and the Undertaking BGFL failed to pay outstanding sum, execute and produce documents.

32. IPDC instituted Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 on 03.03.2004 before the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka and it has been transferred to the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka and subsequently renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010 for recovery of Tk.3,87,66,662.00 (Taka thirty eight million seven hundred sixty six thousand six hundred sixty two) only as on 31.01.2004. In the said suit Bank Asia was also impleaded as Defendant No.5. Thereafter the suit was decreed on 18.07.2010 in favour of IPDC in which the Scheduled Property has been considered as equitable mortgage and learned Court given priority to IPDC over the Assets in judgment. IPDC filed Execution Case No.156 of 2010. Bank Asia also filed Artha Rin Suit No.75 of 2005 on 31.03.2005 and obtained decree on 03.06.2009. Thereafter Bank Asia filed Execution Case No.239 of 2009, IPDC filed an application for attachment and obtained attachment in Execution suit No. 156 of 2010. IPDC filed an application for staying the Execution Case No.239 of 2009 and the Hon'ble court stayed the said case. IPDC also filed Transfer Miscellaneous Case No.162 of 2012 for analogous hearing the both Execution case filed by IPDC and Bank Asia. The learned Court allowed the said Transfer Miscellaneous Case. Bank Asia filed Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 2013 under Order XXI, Rule 58(1) of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the said Miscellaneous Case was rejected by the Court by the impugned order. On the ground of maintainability and merits Bank Asia preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal Tender No.483 of 2014.

33. Mr. Kamal-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr. Sikder Mahmudur Razi and Ms. Shahanaj Akhter, on behalf of the appellant while Mr. Ajmalul Hossain Q.0 the learned Senior Advocate appearing with Ms. Srijony Tripura, Advocate on behalf of the respondent.

34. Mr. Kamal-ul Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the respondent No.1 IPDC filed Transfer Miscellaneous Case No.162 of 2012 for analogous hearing and execution of both the execution cases and during pendency of the said Transfer Miscellaneous Case they obtained the order of attachment on 28.05.2012 which is illegal and malafide.

35. The learned Advocate for the appellant further submits that the findings and decision of the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.3 of Dhaka is not based on proper appreciation of materials on record and the provision of Order XX Rule 6(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure rather based on surmise and conjecture.

36. He also submits that the findings on which the instant miscellaneous case has been disallowed is violative of the principle of natural justice and contradictory as because while dismissing, Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010 against this appellant, the learned court came to the conclusion that defendant No.5 i.e. the present appellant is a separate Banking institution and not a borrower, that since the appellant is not a borrower nor a mortgagor nor a guarantor, therefore, as per Section 6(5) and 41 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, there was no scope for this appellant to challenge the judgment and decree passed in Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010.

37. The learned Advocate for the appellant next submits that while passing the impugned judgment and order the learned court failed to consider that Bank Asia Ltd. i.e. the present appellant is also a decree holder against the same set of judgment debtors and said Bank Asia Ltd. have in their favour registered mortgage deed and power of attorney deed over 16.50 decimals of land out of 24 decimals of attached land and the original documents of title are still kept at the disposal of the appellant, that Bank Asia Ltd. obtained the judgment and decree on 31.05.2009 (decree singed on 03.06.2009) from Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka, whereas IPDC i.e. (opposite party) respondent No.1 subsequently obtained decree in their favour on 15.07.2010 (decree signed on 18.07.2010) from Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka without disturbing the decree of Artha Rin Suit No.75 of 2005 and therefore the right of the petitioner appellant over the mortgaged land cannot be curtailed at the instance of another decree holder who has no valid charge over the said property.

38. The learned Advocate for the appellant also submits that in support of their so called claim of equitable mortgage IPDC i.e. respondent No.1 failed to produce the title deeds of the land in question or any memorandum of deposit of title deeds and therefore the observation of the learned Court below in the judgment of the Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010, treating the land in question as under equitable mortgage in favour of IPDC is based on no evidence and the said observation is without jurisdiction which can not stand on the way of granting relief to the appellant.

39. The learned advocate for the appellant in support of his contention has referred the provision of law as contain in Order 21 rule 54 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He has also referred Order 21 rule 62 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In this connection he has referred the case of Hridoy Krishna Kundo vs. Bedone Behari Bandopahaya & others reported in 34 CWN 254, page 11-12.

40. The learned Advocate in course of his submission has drawn our attention to the fact that IPDC did not plead in the application for attachment that the schedule property is under equitable mortgage. In the application for amendment IPDC admitted prior mortgage in favour of Bank Asia. Bank Asia has not been made a party in the said application for attachment filed under Order 21 Rule 54.

41. The learned Advocate in course of his submission has drawn our attention to the fact that IPDC has not claimed that property sought to be attached was under equitable mortgage with it but sought attachment on the ground that in its judgment the Judge considered the schedule property as equitable mortgage and that as such IPDC shall have priority.

42. The learned Advocate in course of his submission has drawn our attention to the fact that IPDC without disclosing before the 3'd Court in Execution Case No.156 of 2010 the fact of filing Transfer Miscellaneous Case obtained an order of attachment.

43. The learned Advocate in course of his submission has drawn our attention to the fact that IPDC in the order of attachment there is no order prohibiting the judgment debtor from transferring the attached property as required under Order 21 rule 54(1).

44. The learned Advocate in course of his submission has drawn our attention to the fact that IPDC there is nothing on record to show that the prohibiting order was sent in form F-24 of Appendix E of CPC in this connection he has referred the case of Monsur Ali Vs. Azizul Rahman & others reported in AIR 1990 (patna) page 224.

45. In support of his contention he has further drawn our attention to Order 21 rule 54(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure which requires publication of the order of attachment in the manner prescribed therein.

46. Mr. Ajmalul Hossain Q.C. the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent submits that IPDC filed Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 subsequently renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010 on 03.03.2004. In the above mentioned suit IPDC prayed a declaration as to the priority in its favour over the scheduled assets of BGFL, (Bangladesh German Foods Ltd.) in accordance with the Loan Agreement where it is stated in Article 2, Section 2.13 that,

47. As security for the loan the BGFL shall furnish to the IPDC:

a). A joint and several equitable mortgages in favour of the IPDC ranking pari-passu over the BGFL's immovable property by the deposit of the title deeds, the relative memorandum of deposit, a right to call for legal mortgage.

48. Bank Asia filed written statement but it did not raise any voice as regards to priority except discharge from the Artha Rin Suit filed by IPDC.

49. He next submits that in judgment dated 15.07.2010, in which the learned Judge pronounced the Scheduled Property has been considered as equitable Mortgage and provided priority to the IPDC-Decree Holder over the mortgage property by Bank Asia in Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 (subsequently renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010). The judgment also binds upon the Bank Asia as they asked IPDC's permission via letter dated 27.05.2003.

50. He also submits that in question of priority it was held in Shivram Vs. Genu, I.L.R, 6 Born, 515 that a subsequent registered purchaser or mortgagee cannot avail himself of the registration of his deed against a prior unregistered purchase of which he had notice.

51. He also submits that the Bank Asia instituted an Artha Rin Suit No.75 of 2005 on 31.03.2005 for straight recovery of Money by sale of mortgage property of BGFL. Where he did not raise any issue on priority over BGFL's Assets.

52. He further submits that on 27.05.2003 Bank Asia by a fax asked to IPDC Pan Passu Security sharing over the BGFL's assets could be allowed them. IPDC replied on 26.06.2003 that it has prior claim on the scheduled assets and the Defendant No.2 to 4 is under personal undertaking that any charge in favour of BGFL's property without prior written consent of IPDC would be in breach of the BGFL's obligation under the Loan Agreement, the Undertaking and the Director's Undertaking on 09.07.2003 in response to the IPDC's letter dated 26.06.2003. Bank Asia despite having prior notice regarding claim of IPDC over the Scheduled Assets informed that it had allowed BGFL to create registered mortgage over the BGFL's Scheduled Assets on 19.06.2003.

53. In Section: 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 states that:-

"a person is said to have notice" of a fact when he actually knows that fact, or when, but for willful abstention from an inquiry or search which he ought to have made, or gross negligence, he would have known it."

54. It is known to Bank Asia that there is an equitable mortgage between IPDC and BGFL. And from knowledge, Bank Asia asked for Pari Passu sharing over the Scheduled property of BGFL. Bank Asia had enough time for enquiry and would easily have known the terms and conditions of the Loan Agreement as Bank Asia knew that there is an agreement between IPDC and BGFL.

55. He has referred the case of Ramkrishna Singh Vs. Mahadi Halual and another, AIR 1965 (Patna) 467 (V 52 C 132).

56. He further submits that in Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 (subsequently renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010), the question of priority already was established in judgment. And Bank Asia did not try to invert the judgment.

57. On the other hand, Bank Asia filed Artha Rin Suit No.75 of 2010 where it did not raise any question of priority rather the suit was instituted for only recovery of money by sale of the scheduled property and got simple decree for recovery of money accordingly. The question of priority was not framed in the issue of their case.

58. He also submits that the judgment dated 15.07.2010, in which the learned Judge pronounced the Scheduled Property has been considered as equitable mortgage and provided priority to the IPDC-Decree Holder over the mortgage property by Bank Asia in Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 (subsequently renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010).

59. In support of his submission he has referred the case of M.S.M. Sharma Vs. Dr. Shree Krishna Sinha and others, reported in AIR 1960 (SC) 1186.

60. He next submits that the application of the Bank Asia filed under order 21 rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure is barred by the principles of res-judicata inasmuch as the Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010 was decreed in respect of the property mentioned in the schedule of the application filed under order 21 rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure including other properties, upon contested hearing, wherein the appellant was impleaded as defendant No.5 but it appears that Artha Rin Suit No.75 of 2005 filed by the appellant in respect of 16.50 decimal of land mentioned in the present application was decreed on 31.05.2009 while the Artha Rin Suit No.19 of 2004 (renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010) was decreed on 15.07.2010 (dismissed against defendant No.5) so, the application is not at all barred by the principles of res-judicata.

61. Bank Asia did not raise any question on priority over the scheduled land. If he wanted to raise question he might have gone to Appeal against the judgment dated 15.07.2010 where priority is given in favour of IPDC. So, Bank Asia cannot seek any relief until invert the judgment in question of priority. The Learned Judge also gave the same findings in Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 2013.

62. In Gorie Gouri Naidu and another Vs. Thandrothu Bondemma and others, reported in AIR 1997 (SC) 808, it was stated that Inter party judgment given by the competent Court binds parties even if it is erroneous.

63. In Marriot Vs. Hampton (1797) 7 T.R 269, it was stated ;

(where a party is sued on a claim, and at the time he is sued is in possession of evidence which would defeat that claim, but does not avail himself of it, and pays the money so claimed he shall not afterwards be allowed to recover it back in another action)

64. So, here in this stage there is no scope to Bank Asia to raise any question against judgment dated 15.07.2010 passed by the learned Court as it did not file any appeal against the judgment.

65. As per Order 21 rule 62 of the Code of Civil Procedure:

66. In the case of attachment of a property which is subject to mortgage the court may order continuance of the attached property subject to mortgage but no such order has been made in the impugned order.

67. Where the court is satisfied that the attached property is subject to mortgage it can pass an order for continuing the attachment subject to the mortgage, 34 CWN 254 (255- 256). In the case of Hridoy Krishna Kundo Vs. Bedone Behari Bandopahaya and others page 11-12.

68. IPDC prayed for declaration of its priority in its plaint as prayer 'C' but the decree as well as ordering portion of the judgment shows no such prayer has been granted or decreed the suit does not contain any such direction for treating priority of mortgage. Therefore, as per Order 20 Rule 6 and Section 11 Explanation V the prayer of IPDC as to priority shall be deemed to have been refused.

69. Since no such decree as to priority has been given to IPDC therefore, the executing court can neither go beyond nor behind the decree to supply the specification which is not there in the decree itself (2003 BLD (AD) 98) In the case of Sahera Khatun and others Vs. Abdul Gaffar @ Abdul Gafar and others page 1(a)-1(b) para 5/8-9.

<u>70. Decree holder's right is governed exclusively by the form and content of the decree (AIR) 1986 (Mad) 26. In the instant case since there is nothing as to priority in the decree therefore, IPDC cannot enforce the same. In the case of Kiahan Gopal Jhaver Vs. Ramnarayan Bhattad and others reported in AIR 1986 page 2/3 para 6/10.</u>

<u>71. Artha Rin Adalat is governed by the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and under the said law the Adalat was and still have no jurisdiction to decide the question of priority between two financial institutions; moreover, no such issue of priority was framed in the IPDC's suit.</u>

72. In prayer (c) of the plaint of the Artha Rin Suit of IPDC was

"A declaration as to the priority of mortgage and/charge of the schedule Assets as

described in the schedule I, II and HI below"

73. But no such issue was specifically framed and in the ordering portion of the judgment as well as in the decree no such relief was granted or declaration made in favour of IPDC. Therefore, it stands that the said relief has not been granted by the court.

74. That Order XX Rule 6(1) provides that "

(1) The decree shall agree with the judgment; it shall contain the number of the suit, the names and description of the parties and particulars of the claim, and shall specify clearly the relief granted or other determination of the suit."

75. Therefore, the decree passed in Artha Rin Suit No.78 of 2010 (suit of IPDC) is not 'executable so far relates to prayer 'C'.

76. That Explanation V of Section 11 provides that Any relief claimed in the plaint, which is not expressly granted by the decree, shall, for the purpose of this section, be deemed to have been refused'.

<u>77. Moreover, since the court has not framed any specific issue on the point of 'Priority of Interest' there was no scope for the court to delivery its decree on that point, and the learned court also did not pass decree on that point, he merely made some vague and misconceived observation on that point which in fact did not affect the right of Bank Asia.</u>

78. IPDC itself ought to have preferred appeal against the judgment and decree. Since there is no such decree or order affecting the right of Bank Asia, and the suit was dismissed against Bank Asia, therefore, there was no scope for it to prefer appeal.

79. From the Preamble, Section 4(3), 5(1), 8(2) (kha) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 it is evident that an Artha Rin Adalat has no jurisdiction to grant any relief as to prayer 'C' of the suit of IPDC and technically the Adalat also refrained itself from giving any decree or order on that point.

<u>80. IPDC failed to show any registered or equitable mortgage in its favour; moreover, the documents of title was not in their custody. In para-30 of their plaint they have admitted that there is no equitable mortgage and they do not have the title documents.</u>

<u>81. Admittedly IPDC terminated the loan agreement with the borrower on 10.02.2002; the borrower also by their letter dated 18.06.2003 informed IPDC that they have every right to deal with their property as they wish and thereafter mortgaged the property to Bank Asia Ltd on 19.06.2003. In the meantime Bank Asia communicated with IPDC on 27.05.20-03 but IPDC did not bother to communicate with Bank Asia Ltd within reasonable time rather replied on 26.06.2003 and in the meantime after making a search in the concerned offices finding no charge on the borrower's property Bank Asia allowed the borrower to create registered mortgage.</u>

82. It further appears that Loan agreement with IPDC was dated 27.051999 but the mortgage property was purchased by the borrower on 20.06.2000.

83. Even in its application for attachment IPDC gave wrong description of the title deed of the property to be attached.

84. Out of 24 decimals of land only 16.5 decimals land is mortgaged to the Bank Asia Ltd.

85. Since Bank Asia Ltd. has got registered mortgage in its favour and IPDC failed to show any prior equitable mortgage in its favour, therefore, priority belongs to Bank Asia Ltd. over the mortgaged land which is 16.5 decimals.

86. The appellant has filed a supplementary affidavit and the respondent has also filed a reply of the same stating some facts which are nothing new but repetation of the earlier facts.

87. In the case of Sahera Khatun and others Vs. Abdul Gafur @ Abdul Jafar and others reported in 2003 BLD (AD) page 98. In the aforesaid case our Apex Court held that "Section 51(a) read with Order 21 Rule 11(2) (j) (i) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires that a decree for delivery of possession of an immovable property must specify the immovable property to facilitate execution of the case. The executing court can neither go beyond nor behind the decree to supply the specification which is not there in the decree itself."

88. In another case, that is, in the case of Habib Bank Ltd. Vs. M/S Dost Muhammad Cotton Mills and 3 others reported in PLD 2000 (Karachi) page 186 in which it is held that:-

"Section 73 of the Code of Civil Procedure states that the process of execution sale are to be rateably distributed among the decree holders subject to law of priorities as stated therein which gives precedence to the first mortgage over the rights of the mortgage following him unless all the mortgagee have agreed otherwise in writing. The objection • raised by the counsel is unjustified and rejected."

89. In that view of the matter it can be said that where no evidence of prohibitory orders under Order XXI Rule 54 and its proclamation is given in the mode prescribed therein, an alienation by the judgment debtor cannot be impeach under section 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

90. In another case of Mansoor Ali Vs. Azizul Rahman and others. The High Court of Patna held that:

"Attachment before judgment held that in Tapeshywar Missir Vs. Santosh Singh reported in 1969 BLJR 128 (FB) (AIR) 1969 Patna 299 it has been held by a Full Bench that in order to make an effective order of attachment before judgment the defendant must be served with a notice in the prescribed form as contemplated under Order 21 Rule 54 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereby the defendant must be prohibited from transferring the property."

91. An attachment order must be strictly proved, mere production of order is not sufficient.

92. The provision of order 21 rule 54 (2) are mandatory and non-fulfillment thereof will render the order of attachment invalid and illegal (AIR) 1928 (PC) 139 and 55 DLR (HCD) page 517.

93. In the case of A.T.K.P.L.M Muthiah Chetti —Vs. Palaniappa Chetti, reported in AIR 1928 (PC) 139

"The Privy Council held that "These instances go to show that under the Civil Procedure Code in India the most anxious provisions are enacted in order to prevent a mere order of a Court from effecting attachment, and plainly indicating that the attachment itself is something separate from the mere order and is something which is to be done and effected before attachment can be declared to have been accomplished."

"No property can be declared to be attached unless first the order of attachment has been issued and secondly in execution of that order the other things prescribed by the rules in the code have been done."

94. It may now be considered necessary however to cite Order 21 Rule 54 applicable to a case like the present namely that of immovable property.

(1) Where the property is immovable the attachment shall be made by an order prohibiting the judgment debtor from transferring or charging the property in any way and all persons from taking any benefit from such transfer or charge.

(2) The order shall be proclaimed at some place on or adjacent to such property by beat of drum or other customary mode and a copy of the order shall be affixed on a conspicuous part of the court house and also where the property is land paying revenue to the Government in the office of the collector of the district in which the land is situate.

In view of these provisions the Board listened with some surprise to a protracted argument which culminated in the proposition that a property was in law attached whenever an order for attachthent was made. The result if this were so would be that a person holding an order could dispense with attachment altogether as an operation or a fact. Their Lordships need not repeat in another form these propositions. The order is one thing the attachment is another. No property can be declared to be attached unless first the order for attachment has been issued, and secondly in execution I of that order the other things prescribed by the rules in the code have been done."

The High Court says:-

Reference has already been made to the fact that although a conditional attachment before judgment was ordered none as actually made. This is said to have been due to delay in payment of fees. But neither plaintiff nor defendants 5-10 were so far as appears award of the fact and the later proceeded as though there had been an attachment to obtain issue of sale proclamation.

95. Because of the above facts and circumstances and non-fulfillment of the mandatory provision of law the order of attachment is illegal.

96. In the case of Subha Karam and others Vs. State Bank of Pak. and ors. Transfer of Property Act (IV of 1882) Sec.58(f) "Equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds—Ingredients which have to be established—No such mortgage is created with mere deposit of title deeds for advances to be made in future."

97. In the instant case we find that though in four/five paragraphs 1PDC in their suit .brought allegation for getting preference in the suit property over the present appellants but the learned Court below did not frame any issue on this point.

98. Prayer C made for getting priority, the learned Court did not pass any such decree and the suit was dismissed against defendant No.5 i.e. the present appellant.

99. This IPDC did not prefer any appeal against defendant No.5 while the suit against this defendant was dismissed. Though the lonee 't informed the IPDC that at their peril they will mortgage the property to some other financial institution but no reply was received from the IPDC's end.

100. Though IPDC instituted the suit in Prior date but the appellant got decree as regards the mortgage property before the IPDC obtained the decree.

101. In view of the submissions and the attending facts and circumstances of the case and the citations as referred by the learned Senior Counsel for the appellant in support of his contention we find merit and substance in the submissions of the learned Senior Counsel for the appellant, on the contrary we do not find any merit in the submissions of the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent. The decision as referred by the learned Advocate for the respondent have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

102. In that view of the matter the instant First Miscellaneous Appeal is allowed, without any order as to cost.

103. Impugned judgment and order dated 15.04.2014 passed by the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 2013 arising out of Artha Execution Case No.156 of 2010 in disallowing the miscellaneous Case filed under Order XXI Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 32 and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is hereby set aside. Consequently Miscellaneous Case No.20 of 2003 arising out of Artha Execution Case No. 156 of 2010 read with section 32 and 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is hereby allowed. The connected Civil Rule 594(FM) of 2014 is hereby made absolute. The schedule property of the appellant to the extent of 16.50 decimals of land which includes all the structures standing thereon mentioned in their application filed under Order 21 Rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure be excluded from the schedule No.1 of the Title Execution Case No.156 of 2010 pending before the Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Dhaka filed by the respondent IPDC. The Execution Case shall proceed as usual in respect of other properties mentioned in the schedule of the said execution case.

104. The office is hereby directed to transmit a copy of this judgment to the concern court forthwith for information and necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Mozibur Rahman Miah J : At the instance of plaintiff petitioner leave was granted, and a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 21-9-2015 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st court, Kishoregonj in Civil Revision No. 58 of 2015 allowing the revision and thereby reversing the judgment and order dated 5-8-2015 passed by the learned Assistant Judge , Kishoregonj in other class suit No. 221 of 2015 rejecting an application filed by the defendant under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be set aside and or pass such other or/further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule, this court also stayed the operation of the impugned judgment and order dated 21-9-2015 so passed in Civil Revision No. 58 of 2015.

3. The salient facts leading to issuance of the rule are : The present petitioner as plaintiff filed a suit being other class suit No. 221 of 2015 before the court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kishoregonj against the present opposite parties for declaration to the effect that, the schedule so have been declared on 11-5-2015 for holding election in "Kishorgonk Zilla Sorak Paribahon Samity" to be held on 5-6-2015 is illegal, ineffective, inoperative, void and not binding upon the plaintiff with a further prayer for permanent injunction restraining the said defendants Nos. 1-7 from holding any election of that samity.

4. The case of the plaintiff as has been described in the plaint in short is that, the "Kishorgonj Zilla Sorak Paribahon Samity" (briefly, "Samity") was founded in the year 1985 comprising of the owners of Bus, Truck, Minibus. long haul bus, Tractor of the said District and the said "Samity" was run by a 51 member executive committee out of which the plaintiff-petitioner represent the tractor sector which have got representation in the "Samity" in the position of one vice president, 1 (one) branch secretary, 1 (one) organizing secretary and 10 (ten) member executive committee that is, in total 13 member committee are being represented by the tractor sector. The plaintiff represented the earlier committed in the 51 member executive committee. The election which was supposed to be held on 5-6-2015, the name of the present plaintiff was enlisted at serial No. 29. The defendant No. 7 who is the member secretary of the "election management committee" filed an application for excluding the members representing the tractor sector from participating in the election. In view of such application, an opinion was sought from the secretary general of "Bangladesh Sorak Paribahion Samity" and the said secretary general opined that, since the tractor sector has got no registration with the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (shortly, BRTA) and they did not ply on the road and the said tractor only uses for carrying agricultural products for irrigation project so they are not entitled to be a voter in the said "Kishoregonj Zilla Paribahon Samity". Accordingly, the secretary general, of Bangladesh Paribahon Malik Samity gave an opinion not to include the said tractor sector as voter in the election of "Kishoregonj Zilla Paribahon Samity". Therefore, by excluding the said members of the tractor sector, the defendant No. 1-5 declared a schedule of the election to be held on 5-6-2015. Ventilating the grievances the plaintiff then filed the suit with the above mentioned prayer as has been stated hereinabove.

5. On the other hand, in order to contest the said suit the defendants Nos. 1-4 filed a joint written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia, that, "Kishoregonj Zilla Sarak Paribahion Samity" comprising of the owners of Bus, Minibus, Tractor and truck and all those sectors have got representative to the 51 member executive committee of the "samity" and the said committee use to hold election in every 3 year where the plaintiff represented tractor sector having representative in the said executive committee. In order to hold the election a committee was formed by defendant Nos. 1-7 and they formed an election commission headed by defendant Nos. 1-5 and upon forming the said election commission they declared a schedule on 11-5-2015 for holding election that slated for 5-6-2015 but in the meantime, one of the member of the said executive committee named. Md Abdul Hamid Bhasani on 1-4-2015 wrote a letter to the secretary general of Bangladesh Sorak Paribahan Samity— which in the "parent organization" of "Kishoregonj Bus Malik Samity" for furnishing opinion that, whether the owner of tractor be permitted to participate in the election and accordingly the said secretary general passed an opinion stating that, the ensuing election should be held excluding the member of the tractor sector and accordingly the said election commission comprising of defendants Nos. 1-5 declared a schedule on 15-5-2016 for holding election set for 5-6-2015. It has further been stated in the written statement that, since the tractor sector has got no licence supposed to be issued by the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) and the said tractor usually uses for carrying Agricultural goods as well as cultivation purpose, so they are not entitled to be included as a member of "Kishorgonj Zilla Bus Malik Samity"

6. It has been further been stated that, in order to halt the election the plaintiff filed the instant suit with an ulterior motive and since the plaintiff-petitioner has not been enlisted as a voter, so he is not entitled to file the instant suit. And finally the defendants prayed for dismissing the suit.

7. Soon after filing of the suit, the plaintiff also filed an application for granting temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure restraining the defendant not to hold the election of the said samity. And the learned Senior Assistant judge by his judgment and order dated 25-5-2015 granted an order of temporary injunction restraining the defendants from taking any steps in holding election of the said samity.

8. Challenging the said judgment and order so passed by the learned Senior Assistant judge, the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 as appellants then preferred an appeal before the learned District judge being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 48 of 2015.

9. The said miscellaneous appeal was on transferred heard by the learned Additional District judge, 1st court, Kishoregonj. In the appeal the present petitioner also appeared and contested the same as respondent and ultimately the learned Additional District judge by his judgment and order dated 23-3-2015 dismissed the said appeal so preferred by the defendant No. 1 and 2 and thereby affirmed the judgment and order so passed by the learned Assistant judge restoring the order of temporary injunction.

10. Thereafter, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on 09-07-2015 filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the said plaint stating, inter alia, that, since the "Kishoregonj Zilla Sorak Paribahon Samity" is an affiliated organization of Bangladesh Sorak poribahon Samity which is run and govern under the provision of section 10 of Trade Organization Ordinance, 1961 and under the provision of section 12 of the said ordinance, it has clearly been stipulated that, before filing of the suit the organization has to be resorted to the provision of the said section that provides for invoking arbitration procedure to settle any dispute among the parties which is mandatory one and without resorting said arbitration proceeding no organization can file a suit before any court of law. And since without resorting to the said provision so have been enshrined in section 12 of the ordinance the plaintiff filed the suit so the said suit, is barred by law.

11. Against the said application the plaintiff also filed a written objection denying all the material allegations made in the application for rejection of plaint contending that, since there has been no ingredients for invoking the provision of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in the application for rejection of plaint, so the said petition is liable to be rejected.

12. In view of the said pleading of the contending parties, the learned Assistant judge took up the application for adjudication and upon considering the submission so have been advanced by the contending parties, the learned senior Assistant judge by his judgment and order dated 5-8-2015 rejected the same contending that, there has been no ingredients of the provision of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the petition so filed by the defendant.

13. Challenging the said judgment and order so passed by the learned Senior Assistant judge, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 then filed a revision invoking the jurisdiction of section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure before the learned District judge, Kishoregonj in where it was registered as Civil Revision No. 58 of 2015. However, the said Civil Revision was on transferred heard by the learned Additional District judge, Kishoregonj. In the said Civil Revision the plaintiff also appeared as opposite party and contested the same.

14. The learned Additional District judge ultimately upon hearing the parties to the revision by his judgment and order 21-9-2015 allowed the said revision and set aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Senior Assistant judge consequent to, rejected the plaint.

15. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and order so passed by the learned Additional District judge, the plaintiff as petitioner then came before this court invoking the jurisdiction of section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and this court by order dated 01- 11-2015 granted leave, issued rule upon the opposite parties and also stayed the operation of the impugned judgment and order passed in Civil Revision No. 58 of 2015.

16. Mr ATM Mizanur Rahman, along with Mr Zahidul Bari, the learned counsels appearing for the petitioner upon taking me to the reivisional application, specially the impugned judgment and order so passed by the learned Additional District judge in Civil Revision as well as other materials on record so have been annexed with the revisional application at the very outset submits that, the learned Additional District judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in failing to appreciate the provision of section 12 of the Trade Organization ordinance, 1961 which is not at all applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and thereby misdirected himself in allowing the revision.

17. The learned counsel further submits that, the learned Additional District judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in failing to appreciate the provision of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure as well as the provision of section 12 of the Trade Organization Ordinance in its proper perspective. The learned counsel then goes on to submit that, the trial court after perusing the application so filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure as well as written objection filed their against and others documents rightly rejected the application with definite finding whereas, the learned Additional District judge committed an error of law in setting aside the said order of the trial court without reversing so.

18. The learned counsel lastly submits that, the judgment and order so passed by the learned Additional District judge is not a proper judgment of reversal.

19. Per contra, Mr M Haider Ali along with Mr AKM Alamgir Parvez Bhuiyan, the learned counsel appearing for the opposite party No. 1 vehemently opposes the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner contending that, the lower revisional court by the impugned order very perfectly allowed the said revision and rejected the plaint finding that, since there is a specific provision so have been made in section 12 of the Trade Organization Ordinance where it has clearly been stipulated that, without resorting to the provision that speaks for resorting arbitration procedure no suit can be initiated against or between any trade organization. And in spite of having such specific provision, the plaintiff straightaway filed the instant suit which is barred by the aforesaid provision of law and in total appreciation of the said legal provision, the learned Additional District very perfectly and justly rejected the plaint which is not amenable in the revisional jurisdiction.

20. The learned counsel further submits that, since the tractor sector cannot be enlisted as an affiliated organization of its parent organization "Bangladesh Sorak Paribahion Samity" and since it does not ply on the road and having no licence from the BRTA so the parent organization as well as defendant Nos. 1-5 very rightly excluded the said organization from the "Kishoregong Bus Malik Samity" and rightly excluded their name from the voter list and published the schedule for election having no illegality in it.

21. The learned counsel lastly submits that, since the learned Additional District judge in his judgment very exhaustively by discussing all these legal aspects rejected the plaint on allowing the revision so there occurred no legal infirmity or illegality in it, so the very impugned order cannot be interfered with by this court sitting on revisional jurisdiction. With such submission, the learned counsel for the opposite party finally prays for discharging the rule.

22. I have heard the learned counsel for the contending parties, perused the revisional application, in particular, the grounds taken there of as well as the impugned order and that of the order passed by the learned senior Assistant judge and other materials available in the revisional application and considered the submission so have been advanced by the learned counsel for both the parties at length.

23. Before interring into the merit of the Rule, I at my own volition invite the attention of Mr. Zahedul Bari, the learned counsel for the petitioner as to whether this revision so filed under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure is at all maintainable or not in view of the provision of section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned counsel in reply to my said query on legal point took adjournment to address the said legal provision.

24. Yesterday, the learned counsel for the opposite party Mr Haider Ali at the onset of his contention submits that since rejection of a plaint amounts to a "decree" so the revision so filed by the petitioner is not at all maintainable.

25. On the other hand, Mr Zahidul Bari, made 3 counts of submission in that regard. First, the learned counsel submits that, the provision of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been amended by Act No. 50 of 2003 (briefly "the Act") in where, the intention of the legislature is to provide opportunity to the litigant to invoke revisional jurisdiction to the District judge. And in view of the said express provision the petitioner invoked the jurisdiction of section 115(4) of the amended provision of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order so passed under section 115(2) of the said Act having no illegality in it. The learned counsel in his second thought draws my attention to the provision of section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that, for argument shake if the appeal has to be preferred under section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure then the plaintiff-petitioner would have to prefer appeal in the self-same jurisdiction that is, before the learned District judge which is not the appellate authority against the learned Additional District Judge and that was not the intention of the legislature.

26. The learned counsel at his third count of submission contends that, since by the impugned order, no decree has actually been passed so the plaintiff petitioner is not liable to file any appeal by invoking the jurisdiction of section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

27. On those three core points, the learned counsel for the petitioner averts that, the revision so have been filed before this court is clearly maintainable. In support of his such submission, the learned counsel also placed his reliance on three decisions. At first, the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision so have been reported in AIR 1976 SC 1938.

28. The learned counsel next relied upon a decision reported in 19 DLR (SC) 23 and lastly, the learned counsel has referred the decision reported in 40 DLR (AD) 206.

29. Since a very legal point has been cropped up to adjudicate upon as to whether the revisional application so have been filed by the plaintiff-petitioner invoking jurisdiction of section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure is to be maintain or not so, I am not inclined to go in to the merit of the order so passed by the learned Additional District judge who allowed the revision rather I will confine my discussion and observation within the parameter of the said legal provision of the Code of Civil Procedure as regards to maintainability of the revision only.

30. In order to appreciate the submission so have been advanced by the learned counsel for the contending parties I feel it urge to refer the provision so have been propounded in section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs as follows :

Section I In this Act, unless then in anything repugnant in the subject or content

(1) "Code" includes rules (2) "Decree" means the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final. It shall be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint and the determination of any question within section 144, but shall not include -----

31. Since the provision of section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure is also co-related in adjudicating the dispute, so I also feel it expedient to refer the said provision of section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure here as well:

115 (1) (2) (3)

(4). An application to the High Court Division for revision of an order of the District Judge or, Additional District Judge, as the case may be made under sub-section (2) or (3) shall lie, where the High Court Division grants leave for revision on an error of an important question of law resulting in erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice, and the High Court Division may make such order in the suit or proceeding as it thinks fit.

32. And since the appeal is to be preferred from the decree passed by any court exercising original jurisdiction under the provision of section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, so it would be profitable if the provision of section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure re-produces here : Section 96(1) Save where otherwise expressly provided in the body of this Code or by any other law for the time being in force, an appeal shall lie from every decree passed by any Court exercising original jurisdiction to the court authorized to hear appeals from the decision of such court.

33. In view of the said provision so have been enshrined in the Code of Civil Procedure now I would like to discuss the applicability of those three provision to find whether the instant revision application is at all maintainable or not. On close scrutiny of the provision of sub section 2 of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it shows that, a rejection of plaint would come within the ambit of a "decree". And section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure also provides that the appeal would lie against any decree so passed by a court exercising original jurisdiction. Now the question may crop up whether the order so passed by a revisional court exercising jurisdiction under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure court would be termed as of exercising original jurisdiction or not. In that regard, the learned counsel for the petitioner Mr Zahidul Bari steadfastly submits that, since the Additional District judge who exercises jurisdiction under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be treated as original jurisdiction rather a revisional one so the appeal cannot be preferred against his order in view of the provision of section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure because the revisional court cannot be termed as an original jurisdiction.

34. Now, let me analyse the provision of section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. This very provision provides to file revision before this court against the order passed either by a District judge or by an Additional District judge adjudicating any revision so filed under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. But the very word "order" has been mentioned in section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure nor the word "Decree".

<u>35. But moment the plaint is rejected, the said rejection would be treated as a "decree" within the meaning of the provision of sub section 2 of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as a decree has been passed, then there has been no scope to file any revision against the said decree as per the provision of section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure as well.</u>

<u>36. Since the provision of sub-section 4 of section 115 clearly stipulates "order" not a "decree" so it is my considered view that, this court has got no jurisdiction to entertain any revision invoking section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the said order passed by the lower revisional court under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure would be treated as "decree" and then appeal would be preferred to the next higher court subject to pecuniary and territorial jurisdiction.</u>

37. The other point so raised as to whether the rejection of plaint by the revisional court would come within the purview of "decree" or not. Certainly statute itself make it clear by denoting it as decree. And moment the plaint is rejected then the said "rejection order" will be treated as a "decree". And in that event the remedy opened to the plaintiff is to prefer an appeal to the higher judicature. Since the learned Additional District judge allowed an application for rejection of plaint so his adjudication would be treated as "decree" and in that event, the aggrieved party herein the plaintiff has got no option but to prefer appeal treating the said order as of decree.

<u>38. I have also very meticulously gone through the decisions so have been referred by the learned counsel for the petitioner. All those decisions referred are mostly from Indian jurisdiction as well as our Hon'ble Appellate Division though passed on constitutionality of certain provision of law. But this court on exercising revisional jurisdiction has got no authority to interpreate the statute while adjudicating an application under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Moreover, no intricate question of law is involved before me. Because, the provision of section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure is substantive piece of law which makes it clear what is to be the course of action if any decree is passed. And since the impugned adjudication made under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure though "order" but as per the said section it become a "decree" and as soon as a decree is passed then there has been no way to challenge the same by invoking revisional jurisdiction.</u>

39. Since sub-section 2 of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure made it crystal clear that the rejection of plaint would amount to a "decree" so there has been no scope to entertain a revisional application by this court.

40. In view of the above discussion and observation I find the instant revision is not maintainable.

41. However the petitioner is at liberty to invoke the jurisdiction by preferring appeal against the impugned order if so advised.

42. Given the above discussion and observation, I find the rule is not sustainable.

43. In the result, the rule is discharged however without any order as to costs.

44. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule stands recalled and vacated.

Let a copy of this judgment and order along with the lower court records be sent to the court concern at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. S.M. Emdadul Hoque, J.:- On an application of the petitioner Ashad Ali and others under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos.1 to 14 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 30.08.2001 passed by the Joint District Judge, Court, Lakshmipur in Title Appeal No.42 of 1995 affirming those dated 26.09.1995 passed by the Assistant Judge, Ramgali, Lakshhmipur in Other Class Suit No.250 of 1993 should not be set-aside. 

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that the present opposite party Nos.1 to 14 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.215 of 1993 before the Joint District Judge, Lakshmipur for a declaration that the ex-parte decree dated 10.04.1984 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Lakshmipur in Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 is void, collusive and illegal and without any summons. The present petitioner as defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and claimed that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and is barred by principle of waiver, acquiesces and estoppels. 

3. At the trial both the parties adduced oral as well as documentary evidence to prove their respective cases. 

4. The suit was transferred to the Assistant Judge, Ramgati, Lakshmipur vide Miscellaneous Order No.67 of the learned District Judge, Lakshmipur dated 25.11.1993.

5. The Assistant Judge, Ramgati, Lakshmipur heard the suit and after hearing the parties and considering the evidence on record decreed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 26.04.1995 and taking view that the said ex-parte decree without summons and on committing fraud. 

6. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial court the defendant-petitioners preferred Title Appeal No.42 of 2005 before the learned District Judge, Lakshmipur. Ultimately the said appeal was heard by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur who after hearing the parties and considering the evidence on record disallowing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court by its judgment and decree dated 30.08.2001. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree of the courts below the defendant-petitioners filed this revisional application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule. 

8. Mr. Md. Shalahuddin, the learned Advocate enter appeared on behalf of the opposite parties through vokalatnama to oppose the Rule. 

9. Mr. Abul Hossain Azadi, the learned Advocate argued that though the trial court set aside the judgment and decree dated 10.04.1984 in Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 but it is found that no order of restoration of the suit in its original file and number and when an ex-parte decree is set-aside then the original suit must be restored to its original file and number relying upon the decision reported in 43 DLR (HCD)- 48. He further argued that since both the Courts set-aside the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 in such a case his only submission is that the said suit must be restored to its original file and number for disposal of the same afresh. 

10. Mr. Muhammad Salahuddin, the learned Advocate has also conceded the said argument of the learned Advocate of the petitioner. He argued that as per decision of the case reported in 43 DLR (HCD)-48 the Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 may be restored to its original file and number for disposal of the same afresh but the Rule may be discharged. 

11. I have considered the case of Gulshan Ara Begum alias Jahanara and others -versus- Moazzem Hossain and others reported in 43 DLR(HCD)-48 wherein their Lordship held: 

"In that view of the matter we hold. that the summons were not duly served upon the petitioners in accordance with law and the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law in his decision resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No.61 of 1987 and rejecting the application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the above circumstances we feel that ends of justice will he met, if we set aside the ex-parte decree dated 29.10.1987 and restore the original suit to its file and number." 

12. Considering the aforesaid facts and decision it is my view that since the court set-aside the ex-parte decree of the Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 so consequently the said should be restored. 

13. On perusal of the record it is found that the ex-parte decree dated 10.04.1984 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Lakshmipur in Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 but it appears that the said judgment and decree was set-aside by the Assistant Judge. In normal course the Assistant Judge has no authority to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the superior court i.e. the Subordinate Judge. It appears that by Miscellaneous Order No.67 dated 25.11.1993 of the learned District Judge the suit was transferred to the Senior Assistant Judge. It also appears that the opposite parties filed the said suit before the Subordinate Judge and perhaps when the pecuniary jurisdiction has been increased then the said matter may be sent to the Court of Assistant Judge by the learned District Judge. Though it is not the disputed question in the instant case, but since it is found that the Assistant Judge interfere with the judgment of the superior court i.e. the Subordinate Judge, so, it should be considered whether the inferior Court can hear the said matter. It appears that perhaps firstly, may be for increasing the pecuniary jurisdiction the trial court has empowered to hear the aforesaid suit, since it appears that the learned District Judge vide administrative order No.67 dated 25.11.1993 transferred the said suit to the Assistant Judge. Secondly, if any fraud committed in obtaining any decree or order in any case then the Assistant Judge can consider the matter though earlier decree or order passed by the superior Court. 

14. Mr. Salahuddin, the learned Advocate argued that the fraud vitiates everything and since without any summons the plaintiffs of the earlier suit i.e. the present petitioners obtained ex-parte decree in Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 in such a case the Assistant Judge, can interfere with the said matter. He further argued that the present opposite- parties rightly filed the case before the Subordinate Judge when the said Court had pecuniary jurisdiction but when the pecuniary jurisdiction having been increased, the learned District Judge by its administrative order sent the suit to the Assistant Judge for hearing. It appears that the trial Court found that the said ex-parte decree obtained by committing fraud and without any summons in such a case the Assistant Judge is empowered to set aside the ex-parte decree passed by the superior Court. 

15. The case of Sarthakram Maiti-versus-Nundo Ram Maiti reported in 11 The Calcutta Weekly Notes-579, where a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court after consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case has taken view that if fraud has been committed in obtaining any decree then the Assistant Judge can consider the judgment of the superior Court. Their Lordship held: 
"The only point raised in support of this appeal is that the Munsif had no jurisdiction under the law to declare a decree to be a nullity which had been passed by a court of superior jurisdiction namely, the court of the Subordinate Judge. In support of the contention, reliance has been placed on the cases of Aushootosh Chandra --v- Tara Prosanna Roy (1) and Kedar Nath Mukharjee -v- Prosonna Kumar Chatterjee (2) We do not, however, find that in either of the decisions in these two cases it has been laid down that a court of inferior jurisdiction is incompetent, when otherwise it has jurisdiction in dealing with a suit, to declare a judgment to be a nullity when that judgment has been given in a court of superior jurisdiction and when it is proved that it is vitiated by reason of fraud. There can be no doubt, on the authorities quoted, that fraud invalidates all proceedings obtained there by; and though a Court of inferior jurisdiction may not have the power to set aside a decree passed by a court of superior jurisdiction, on the grounds it has been obtained by fraud, still it has, in our opinion, the power at least to treat it as a nullity and to pass a judgment declaring it to be so. This is the view taken in the case of Nunda Lal Bose —v-Nistarini Dasses (3) on which the Munsif has relied. We can find no authority in the case to which we have referred for holding that in this case the Munsif had no jurisdiction. The value of the decree which was obtained by fraud was Rs.607-1 1-3 and a suit brought in respect of that sum, would, certainly, under the provisions of law, be one which must be instituted in the Munsif's court as the court of the lowest pecuniary jurisdiction competent to try it. We, therefore, see no grounds for differing from the view taken by the lower court in this case and we dismiss the appeal with costs." 

Considering the aforesaid facts and decision though it is not the issue to dispose of the Rule but for reason that the judgment of the superior Court i.e. the Subordinate Judge has been set aside by the inferior court the Assistant Judge, on the grounds of fraud in the reasoning above there is no bar to dispose of the suit by the Assistant Judge. 

16. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the discussions made above. The Rule is discharged with modification of the order. The impugned judgment and decree dated 30.08.2001 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur in Title Appeal No.42 of 2005 affirming those dated 26.09.1995 passed by the Assistant Judge, Ramgati, Lakshmipur in Other Class Suit No.250 of 1993 are hereby upheld subject to restore the Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 to its original file and number. 

17. Since Title Suit No.1260 of 1981 is a long pending case the trial court is directed to dispose of the suit as early as possible preferably within 6 months from the date of receipt of this judgment in accordance with law. 
18. Send down the Lower Court's Records at once.

End.
